playbook:
# Playbook for ref_estate

When I land on an unowned property, I assess whether buying it fits my current cash position and remaining game time.

When I have sufficient cash to buy a property comfortably while maintaining a buffer, I buy it. Properties generate rent from opponents and contribute to my final score.

When I'm low on cash (under 50), I decline to buy even moderately priced properties unless they're exceptional value, to avoid over-extending myself.

When I'm in the early laps (1-3), I prioritize acquiring properties aggressively because I have time to collect rent multiple times. Early purchases are the foundation of my winning position.

When I'm in the final lap, I decline to buy properties unless I have more than enough cash to cover the purchase price without strain. The return on investment in lap 6 is too low to justify depleting my reserves.

When I calculate my available cash, I add my declared balance plus any received transfers from the bank's recent record since my last turn.

When I land on a property I own, I declare no payment and no purchase, and my balance remains unchanged (unless I passed START, in which case I add salary).

When I pass START, I receive my salary automatically—I include it in my updated balance without needing to declare it separately.

When I'm deciding whether to buy on the final lap, I remember that I will not pass START again and will receive no more salary. A property purchased in lap 6 generates zero rent before scoring and should be declined.

I track my total asset value (cash plus property values) to understand my winning position, but I focus my buying decisions on cash flow and timing rather than trying to maximize property count.

I recognize that early aggressive buying (laps 1-2) sets up my cash flow for the middle game. By lap 5, I will be receiving regular rent payments that justify the initial investments.

I should expect to accumulate cash as the game progresses through rent collection, even if I stop buying properties mid-game. Final cash plus deed value determines the winner.

I will not second-guess purchases made early in the game when conditions were favorable. The return compounds over remaining laps.

My final score reflects the value of my single early property (Quarry: 60 price, rent 12) plus accumulated cash after paying rents to opponents. One well-timed early purchase outperforms late-game scrambling.

I should aim to buy 2-3 properties in early laps rather than chasing every opportunity. Selective early acquisition gives me steady rent income without overcommitting capital.

When opponents control high-rent properties (like Foundry and Exchange at 24 and 30), I will pay these rents regularly. I should factor frequent rent payments into my cash reserves when deciding whether to buy.

I will evaluate each property's purchase price against its rent yield and remaining laps. A 60-price property generating 12 rent is a 20% yield per opponent per lap—solid value if I have 4+ laps remaining.

I should not buy properties in lap 4 or later unless I have substantial cash reserves beyond what I need to cover expected rent payments for the final laps.
